canonical_title: How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later
author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Dick's celebrated 1978 essay-address on reality and authenticity, home to his famous definition: reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away.
page_summary:
Composed as a talk in 1978 and among the most quoted things Dick ever wrote, this essay moves from wry autobiography to metaphysics without ever losing its conversational footing. Dick opens by admitting that his whole career has consisted of building fake universes for a living, then asks what happens when the fakes prove more durable than the real. His touchstone line, "reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away," anchors a broader worry about how governments, media, and corporations manufacture pseudo-realities that people inhabit unknowingly.

The piece also turns confessional, recounting the disorienting religious and perceptual experiences of 1974 that fed his Exegesis, and it treats the authenticity of the human being as the real stake behind the authenticity of the world. Androids, simulations, and counterfeit environments matter because they test whether a person remains genuinely alive inside them.

The portal holds two archive manifestations of the essay. It stands as the accessible front door to Dick's late philosophy and is often read alongside "The Android and the Human" and the Exegesis selections.
